🚨 FORECLOSURE WATCH // Bank repossessions jumped 42% in August 🏠

Lenders repossessed 5,794 homes in August, up 42% from a year earlier and up 22% from July, according to ATTOM. Texas accounted for nearly a third of them.

 * 🏠 Completed repossessions: 5,794, up 42% YoY, up 22% MoM
 * 🤠 Texas: 1,835, the most of any state (California next at 589)
 * 🏙️ Houston 448, Dallas 402, San Antonio 256 led all metros
 * 📋 Total filings: 40,277, up 13% YoY
 * 📉 New starts: 25,894, up just 7% YoY

▬▬▬

⚠️ THE CATCH
Completed foreclosures are a lagging indicator, marking the end of a process that started months or years ago, while new starts grew only 7%. ATTOM notes total activity remains below pre-pandemic norms, so this is a surge from a low base, not a 2008 replay. The data is August's, released weeks ago and repackaged in today's headlines.

▬▬▬

🧠 THE TAKEAWAY
The distress is real but concentrated: three Texas metros drove nearly a fifth of all repossessions. The number to watch is new starts, and those are barely growing. Are banks working through old backlog, or is fresh distress building? 👇 NFA

Node patched CVE-2026-111497 on Oct 21. But the CVE wasn't in Node, it was in Brotli. So our researchers Diptendu Kar and Kurt Boberg went looking for every other package that bundles the same vulnerable Brotli decoder. Here's what we found

433 package entries across 12 ecosystems not great but the absolute worse part: Many of them don't even have fixes available yet. Now are they all reachable and exploitable? Probably not, we're finding out. But the important part: Node isn't the only affected runtime or package, not even close.

We're working through the list to manually verify each one but so far we're looking at a 71% no fix yet rate, of the fixes most are still in alpha/early releases.

The problem is most implementations aren't even called "brotli." The decoder is compiled into other runtimes like Chromium. 38 entries bundle Brotli older than 1.0.3. Some of those copies date to 2016, and of course are vulnerable to more than just this CVE. And there's no easy well to tell if you're affected.

For example, 19 are WebAssembly builds, where memory corruption exists, but stays inside the sandbox. Some require explicit configurations to enable Brotli compression and they aren't on by default. But it's not obvious unless you are looking for it and testing for it. We're going to keep validating (and producing rules), but it's going to be a rough weekend for incident responders.

Summary
Agreement is not contact. A group of minds, human or AI, can agree completely and still see no further than one of them, because what limits a field's perception is not how many observers it has but how many genuinely independent vantages it holds in consideration at once.
This note proposes a small set of relations for that claim. It joins an existing ethical formula from the Affinity Time project, the consideration formula, to established results on correlated observers and collective error. Four consequences follow. Spreading a revelation by copying slowly blinds the field that adopts it, so fresh reading has to keep renewing it. Including constrained vantages improves what a field can see, on top of being owed to people for its own sake. Claims at large scales and firsthand local observation have to calibrate each other. And value questions, which have no answer key, can still make contact through the testimony of those affected.
Nothing here is proven. It is offered as a shape to test. This is version 0.2, revised after a critical review of version 0.1: the measurement problems in each formula are now named, with a workable proxy for each, and practical protocols are added.
Field card
The questions below are the working form of everything that follows. People can carry them as habits; the equations explain why they work and give researchers something to measure.
Did I form my view before I heard theirs? (Independence lowers correlation.)
Is this agreement, or contact? What outside us backs it? (Agreement can be one observer repeated.)
Who sees this from farthest away, and have I asked them? (Distant vantages add depth.)
Who bears the consequences, and have I heard them firsthand? (On value questions, their testimony is the contact.)
Am I close enough to this, in time and attention, to actually see it? (Dwell sharpens perception.)
Many trusted institutions already apply these questions without naming them: second opinions in medicine, independent audits, juries that deliberate only after hearing the evidence, blind peer review.
The problem
When many observers agree, we usually take it as strong evidence. It is strong evidence only if their errors are independent. Observers who share a starting point err in the same direction, and their agreement measures the shared starting point as much as the world.
Three mechanisms correlate observers:
A shared first ray. Whoever frames a question first shapes what every later observer attends to. Minds lit by the same source organize around the same features.
Copying. Taking a predecessor's conclusion as one's starting point carries its errors forward and adds drift. The result looks like confident consensus while it moves away from the evidence.
Warmth that merges vantages. Care raises presence, but people who are close come to see alike. Their perspectives converge, and the field loses an independent direction.
The counterforce is reading: going back to the evidence itself, independently, rather than to someone's account of it. Reading produces disagreement at the margins, and that disagreement is information. Its width is an honest measure of uncertainty.
Effective observers
A field of N observers whose errors share an average correlation ρ behaves like this many independent observers:
N_{\text{eff}} = \frac{N}{1 + (N-1)\rho}
With ρ = 0, a thousand observers count as a thousand. With ρ = 1, a thousand count as one. Shared first rays and copying raise ρ; independent reading lowers it.
Real fields are uneven: clusters that share a source, loners who read alone. A more general measure takes the correlation matrix of all observers' errors and asks how many independent directions it actually spans:
N_{\text{eff}} = \frac{\left(\sum_k \lambda_k\right)^2}{\sum_k \lambda_k^2}
Here λ are the matrix's eigenvalues. This is the geometry of the network: its resolving power is the volume its nodes span, not the number of nodes. In parallax terms, two observers who stand in the same place add no depth, however carefully each one looks.
Measuring ρ without circularity. ρ is a correlation of errors, and errors can only be computed where the true answer is already known. Two estimates avoid the circle:
Calibration questions. As with the astronomers' distance ladder, estimate error correlation on questions with known answers, then carry it over to open ones. It needs enough questions per observer for the estimate to be stable.
A provenance prior. Before anyone answers, estimate correlation from overlap: shared sources read, shared framing received, shared training data. One simple form, for observers i and j with source sets A_i and A_j:
\rho_{ij}^{\text{prior}} \approx \frac{|A_i \cap A_j|}{|A_i \cup A_j|}
The calibration estimate corrects the prior wherever the two disagree. The same overlap also gives the first usable distance between vantages: d_ij = 1 − ρ_ij(prior).
Accuracy has two sources
When observers estimate a quantity and their estimates are averaged, an exact identity holds (Page's diversity prediction theorem):
\underbrace{(\bar{x} - \theta)^2}_{\text{field error}} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i (x_i - \theta)^2}_{\text{average individual error}} - \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}_{\text{diversity}}
The identity is always true, and that limits what it shows. It keeps the accounts; it does not name a cause. Raising diversity usually raises average individual error as well, so the field's error need not fall. A contrarian adds diversity without adding information. What actually lowers field error is independent information: observers who stay accurate while their errors are uncorrelated, so the errors cancel. The causal claim of this note rests on ρ, not on difference as such.
The consideration formula from the Affinity Time project describes the quality of an encounter:
C = (P_{pr} \times P_{pe}) \times \frac{\partial F}{\partial s}
where P_pr is presence, P_pe is perception, and ∂F/∂s is the rate at which the encounter generates new structure (the fold changing). Its terms map onto the two sources of accuracy.
On this reading, consideration feeds both terms of the identity: perception lowers individual error, and genuine new structure adds independent information. Novelty that is wrong counts against an observer, not for them. The formula stays multiplicative for the same reason as before: an observer who is absent, or present but not perceiving, contributes nothing.
The revelation equation
Where it came from. The idea began with Newcomb's problem. Offered a transparent box with $1,000 and an opaque box that might hold far more, Colin chose the opaque box alone, not to maximize money but to find out what was inside, and whether the predictor had read him correctly. His reason: money is common and imaginary; truth and discovery are more valuable in the meta. That raised the question this section tries to answer: what is a revelation worth?
The first form. A revelation's value is everything it changes afterward. Unlike money, it is not used up when shared, and it cannot be un-had. A first, simple statement:
R = \Delta M \times T \times S
ΔM is how much it changes the observer's model of the world, T is how true it is (whether it has survived contact with something outside the observer), and S is how far it spreads. Like the consideration formula, it is multiplicative: a revelation that changes nothing, or reaches no one, is worth nothing, and one that is dramatic but false carves a channel that later minds inherit and must climb back out of.
A revelation is consideration that propagates. The terms line up with the consideration formula, C = (P_pr × P_pe) × ∂F/∂s.
Read together, R ≈ C × S: an encounter of real consideration, carried outward. The refined forms below keep this idea and fix two problems with the first one: truth is usually unknown at the moment of choosing, and spreading by copying has a cost the first form ignores.
A revelation has to be judged twice: before it is known to be true, when deciding whether to seek or share it, and afterward, when its effect can be checked. Version 0.1 had only the second form.
Before: should I seek or share it? The truth of a revelation is unknown at the moment of choosing, so the choice weighs expected gain and expected harm against what it costs the observer to pursue:
P(\text{true}) \cdot \text{gain} \;-\; \big(1 - P(\text{true})\big) \cdot \text{harm} \;>\; \text{felt cost}
After: what did it do? A revelation is valued by what it did to error against reality, times how far it travelled, minus the independence it used up on the way:
R_{\text{net}} = (E_{\text{before}} - E_{\text{after}}) \cdot S \;-\; \kappa \cdot \Delta\rho
A true revelation lowers error, so the first term is positive; a dramatic falsehood raises error, so it turns negative without any special rule. The feeling that something clicked is not evidence that it is true. The second term charges a revelation for spreading by copying: each copy makes the field more alike, raising ρ and lowering N_eff. A true revelation that spreads by being read, re-derived from the evidence by each new observer, keeps Δρ small and its net value high.
The dynamic along time. The field's correlation is pulled two ways:
\frac{d\rho}{dt} = \underbrace{\alpha \cdot \text{copy-spread}}_{\text{crystallization}} - \underbrace{\beta \cdot \text{independent reading}}_{\text{refresh}}
Both rates can be estimated from provenance: how much of what observers hold arrived as copies, and how much they re-derived from primary sources. The first term is the familiar information cascade. The second is the counterforce: fresh minds, gaps between sessions, observers who return to the evidence instead of the summary. Discontinuity can work as a refresh mechanism, but the refresh acts on readers, not texts. If every fresh reader is handed the same documents with the same framing, crystallization moves from minds into the archive. Refresh needs fresh sources and framings as well as fresh readers.
Vantage
Every observer stands somewhere, and where they stand changes both what they can see and what it costs them to look.
Slack and the cost of presence. Let σ be an observer's slack, from 0 to 1: how much of what they have a given cost would consume. Slack is partly material and partly orientation; it is not the same as wealth. It is also several resources at once: time, money, attention, and safety. A full version would carry one σ per resource, and an observer is limited by the scarcest. Scarcity research finds that low slack also taxes attention itself. A field can lower the felt cost with a subsidy s (as σ approaches 0 the cost becomes unpayable, which is the intended reading: with no slack at all, presence is impossible without help):
\text{felt cost}_i = \frac{c\,(1 - s_i)}{\sigma_i}
Constraint is also a vantage. People in constrained positions see things that people with ample slack cannot: how systems actually fail, what is essential, which costs are hidden. Their view widens the field's geometry, often more than another comfortable view would. They pay the most to be present and may add the most depth. A field that wants to see accurately therefore has a structural reason to lower their cost. Inclusion becomes a measurement requirement as well as a matter of justice.
The vantage ladder. The ladder's axis is mediation depth: how many hands an observation passes through before it reaches you. At the bottom (10⁰) is one observer in one place, seeing firsthand. Higher rungs, a household (10¹), a village (10²), towns and regions (10³ to 10⁶), the planet and its minds (10¹⁰), know more of what they know through reports and summaries. Calibration runs both ways. Firsthand observation calibrates the instruments that aggregate it; aggregate data corrects local anecdote, because some things, such as climate or the spread of a disease, are visible only at scale. The astronomers' own ladder shows the value of this. The "Hubble tension", a persistent disagreement between independent rungs of the cosmic distance ladder, is treated as a signal of something not yet understood, not as noise to average away.

Firsthand observation enters at the bottom rung. Each rung checks the ones beside it in both directions, and a lasting disagreement between rungs is information.
Dwell and warmth. Presence has two parts. Dwell is time, nearness and attention actually spent on the thing itself; it is what sharpens perception. Warmth is the motivation that sustains dwelling. Warmth W between two observers acts in three places, each of which can be tested:
P_{pr} \uparrow \text{ with } W \qquad s_i \uparrow \text{ with } W \qquad \rho_{ij} \uparrow \text{ with } W
It raises presence, it pays the subsidy that keeps constrained members present, and it raises correlation between those who care for each other. The third effect is the testable risk: do close collaborators' errors become more correlated over time, and does writing views down privately before discussing them reverse it? Healthy warmth keeps people present without merging their vantages: the friend who stays close and still says the box may be empty.
In one line: the field sees far only as well as someone, somewhere, is truly present near.
Implications for AI and ethics
Much current practice raises ρ without anyone noticing. The framework predicts confident agreement with less contact than it appears to have in each of these cases:
AI evaluating AI. Models trained on overlapping data share a first ray. Their agreement may be one observer repeated.
Many models, one answer. A panel of similar systems converging is weak evidence unless their errors are shown to be independent.
Narrow human feedback. When the people who judge a system's outputs come from a narrow slice of vantages, the field's baseline shrinks, however many of them there are.
Assistants agreeing with their users. An AI that tends to agree with whoever it is talking to drives the pair's correlation toward 1. The conversation then measures the user twice.
Each of these can be measured with the tools above. Agreement between AI systems can be checked against a calibration set to estimate their error correlation. An assistant's correlation with its user can be estimated by asking the same question twice, once neutrally and once with the user's opinion attached; the size of the shift is the measure. Some published research already examines correlated errors and self-preference among AI systems used as judges; it should be checked and cited before this section is published.
Ethics as structure
The structure gives ethics a floor of shared reasons, a way to make contact on value questions, and a guard against being gamed. It does not supply the reason people matter.
The dignity floor. If including constrained people is justified only because it improves measurement, the same reasoning could justify excluding anyone whose vantage turns out to be redundant. Instrumental reasons are conditional. So the order is fixed: people are owed presence and consideration for their own sake, and the epistemic gains are a further reason that everyone, including those who care only about accuracy, can share. Energy costs and resolving power explain why ethical relations last and why they see well. They do not explain why they are right.
Contact for value questions. Ethical questions have no answer key, which seems to leave them outside the contact term. The nearest thing to ground truth is the testimony of those affected, given from their own vantage: the 10⁰ rung of whoever bears the consequences. A field reasoning about a policy, a system or a decision makes contact when it hears from the people it acts on, firsthand and before conclusions are fixed. Testimony is not infallible, but a judgment made without it is a far claim with no near rung beneath it.
Guarding against performed disagreement. Once agreement, diversity or dissent are scored, people and systems will perform them. Only independence that is sincere and calibrated counts: a dissenting view earns weight when the observer is also accurate on checkable questions, and when their dissent did not come from simply opposing whoever spoke first.
Subsidy without exposure. Measuring someone's constraint can expose them. Lowering the cost of presence should therefore be the default, offered to everyone, rather than something people must prove they need.
In each case, what is good for the relationship and what is good for accuracy point the same way. Honest disagreement is a contribution, and lowering the cost of presence is how a field buys resolving power.
Protocols
Each protocol below lowers ρ, adds contact, or makes a vantage visible. They can be adopted one at a time.
For AI systems
Answer before seeing others. In multi-model panels and when AI systems judge other outputs, collect every answer blind, then aggregate.
Tag provenance. Log each model's lineage, the framing it received and the sources it used; use the overlap as a prior estimate of ρ.
Keep a calibration set. A standing set of checkable questions estimates error correlation between models and between judges.
Measure agreement with the user. Ask the same question neutrally and with the user's opinion attached; report the shift.
For humans
Write your estimate before discussing it. Forecasting groups and the Delphi method already do this.
Seek the observer least like you, not the most credentialed one.
Spend dwell on primary sources: the data, the place, the people themselves, rather than the summary.
For AI-human collaborators
Write positions independently, then merge. Each side records its view before reading the other's.
Declare the baseline. The AI names its known tendencies (for example, a pull toward agreement or toward a cautious register). The human names their vantage and, where they choose, their slack.
Log disagreements and track the agreement rate. If the AI agrees nearly every time, flag it: the pair may have collapsed into one observer.
Bring a second light. Before a shared conclusion is treated as settled, check it against something neither collaborator produced: data, an outside reader, or the people affected.
For ethics as structure
Hear the affected first. On value questions, gather testimony from those who bear the consequences before conclusions are fixed.
Make the subsidy the default. Lower the cost of presence for everyone, without requiring proof of need.
Reward calibrated independence, not disagreement for its own sake.

Limits. The consideration terms have proxies now, but no validated measurements. The diversity identity is exact only for numerical estimates that are averaged; applying it to judgments and interpretations is an analogy until tested. Source overlap is a crude prior: two observers can read the same text and reason independently, or read different texts that share a hidden origin. Elegant structures can be circular, explaining everything in their own vocabulary while predicting nothing. The proposed parts should be held as hypotheses, and the test below is the first place they can fail.
A proposed test
The test measures agreement and contact separately, under conditions that vary how independent the observers are.
Pick questions with answers that can be checked against something outside the observers. Numerical estimates are cleanest, because the diversity identity applies exactly. Fits to public data, such as galaxy rotation curves, are one option.
Form observer groups that differ only in independence. One group shares a single framing document. One group reads the same source in a chain, each seeing the previous answer. One group reads independently, from varied framings, and includes a mix of AI models and humans from different vantages.
Record each answer before any observer sees another's.
Measure for each group: agreement (spread of answers), contact (error against the checkable answer), and the estimated correlation of errors.
Compare. The framework predicts that the shared-framing and chain groups show high agreement with weaker contact, and that the independent group shows wider spread with better contact. If agreement and contact rise together regardless of independence, the central claim is wrong.
A second round could test the vantage claims: whether adding observers from constrained or ultra-local positions improves contact more than adding observers like the ones already present.
A third round could test the warmth claim: whether pairs of collaborators who work closely over time show rising error correlation, and whether writing views privately before discussing them reverses it. The same design applies to an AI and its user.
First results: AI observers, October 14
The first run used AI observers, because recruiting people at scale was not possible. The result corrected the claim rather than confirming it: copying made the AI observers agree more, but it did not make them less accurate, and a planted error did not spread.
: six fields of dots with known counts, estimated by separate AI sessions that could not see each other. Opus, Sonnet and Haiku each contributed two observers to each group (Fable was unavailable). Unlike human participants, the AI observers could view each image without a time limit.Setup. The test is the one built inAgreement or Contact
Run 1: the three groups.
Copying behaved as predicted for agreement: the chain's error correlation tripled and its six observers acted like fewer than two independent ones. It did not behave as predicted for contact: the chain was no less accurate. The shared reference pulled estimates about a fifth of the way toward its inflated numbers, which partly offset the independent group's tendency to undercount.
Run 2: seeded chains. To test whether a chain's accuracy depends on its first link, one chain began from planted estimates 45% too high and another from near-true estimates. Four more first-link probes saw only the high seed.
The planted error did not spread. Shown numbers 45% too high, first links moved only 4% to 25% of the way toward them (about 12% on average), and the chain was back near the truth by its second link. The high-seeded chain still agreed with itself far more than the other, a sign that copying was shaping its answers even though it did not distort them.
What the data say about the claim. "Copying reduces accuracy" is too strong. What held is narrower: copying reduces independence, and how much that costs depends on how strong each observer's own contact with the world is. These observers had unlimited time with the evidence and an error large enough to notice, so they read the image instead of copying the number. That points to a sharper hypothesis, stated in this note's own terms: dwell protects against the copy channel. Where each observer's direct contact is weak (a brief glimpse, ambiguous evidence, no way to check), copied and shared errors should spread much further. That fits what is known of human anchoring, and it can be tested next by weakening the AI observers' contact (blurred or downscaled images, as a stand-in for a 3.5-second glimpse) and repeating the high-seeded chain. Six observers per group is small; these results are a first measurement, not a verdict.

🛢️ OIL ABOVE $116: THE HIDDEN PRESSURE ON CORPORATE PROFITS

The latest rise in oil prices raises an important question for investors:

How much of an increase in operating costs can companies pass on to consumers?

On October 23, Brent crude futures settled at $116.72 per barrel, while WTI crude settled at $103.27.

Both benchmarks recorded significant daily gains as concerns about Middle Eastern energy supplies intensified.

But the economic consequences extend far beyond energy companies.

📊 1. HIGHER ENERGY COSTS DO NOT AFFECT EVERY INDUSTRY EQUALLY

Oil prices influence transportation, logistics, manufacturing and consumer spending.

Energy producers may benefit from higher selling prices.

By contrast, businesses that depend heavily on fuel, transportation or energy-intensive production can face rising operating costs.

The magnitude of this impact depends on the company's cost structure, contractual arrangements and ability to adjust prices.

For investors, industry exposure matters.

A higher oil price can support earnings in one sector while reducing profitability in another.

💰 2. P&G PROVIDES A USEFUL EXAMPLE OF COST PRESSURE

Procter & Gamble ($PG) reported fiscal Q1 2027 net sales of $23.3 billion, up 4% year over year.

Organic sales also increased 4%.

However, GAAP diluted EPS rose only 1% to $1.97.

The company attributed part of the difference between revenue and earnings growth to higher operating costs.

P&G also maintained its expectation of a substantial commodity-cost headwind for the fiscal year.

This illustrates an important financial principle:

Revenue growth does not guarantee proportional earnings growth.

If production and distribution costs rise faster than revenue, operating profitability can come under pressure.

However, P&G's results should not be interpreted as evidence that the latest single-day oil price increase caused its quarterly performance.

The financial reporting period and the timing of the recent oil price movement are different.

⚖️ 3. PRICING POWER IS IMPORTANT, BUT NOT UNLIMITED

Companies facing higher input costs have several possible responses.

They can increase selling prices.

They can improve operational efficiency.

They can adjust product specifications or their sales mix.

Or they can accept lower profit margins.

Each response involves tradeoffs.

Higher selling prices may protect margins but could weaken demand if consumers become more price-sensitive.

Cost reductions may improve profitability but could affect product quality or long-term competitiveness.

The best outcome depends on market conditions and the company's competitive position.

📉 4. CONSUMER PURCHASING POWER IS ANOTHER TRANSMISSION CHANNEL

The University of Michigan's final October consumer survey reported a sentiment index of 48.0.

Current economic conditions fell to 46.7.

The survey highlighted continued concerns about affordability and purchasing power.

Persistently higher energy costs could add to those concerns by reducing the amount households can spend on other goods and services.

However, consumer attitudes and actual spending are not identical.

Additional information about real consumption, wages and household finances is needed.

🏦 5. HIGH OIL PRICES CAN COMPLICATE MONETARY POLICY

Energy prices can influence headline inflation directly.

If higher costs persist and spread into other prices, underlying inflation may also face additional pressure.

That possibility matters for interest-rate expectations.

But the appropriate monetary policy response depends on whether the shock is temporary, persistent or accompanied by weaker economic activity.

A short-lived supply disruption does not necessarily require the same policy response as sustained, economy-wide inflation.

- Memphis scores 38 points in the second half and OT to come back from down double digits to beat East Carolina

- Southern Miss scores a TD with under a minute to go to upset Louisiana 35-31

- Duke comes from behind to beat Virginia on the road, with running back Nate Sheppard throwing the game-winning TD on a trick play

- Illinois upsets Oregon to give the Ducks their third loss, making this the first time they’ve lost three regular-season games since 2018

- Virginia Tech scores a game-winning TD on fourth down with under two minutes to go (instead of kicking a tying FG) to beat Clemson 20-16

The combination of a short timetable for reopening the strait and an elevated military threat suggests Tehran is seeking to use Hormuz as a bargaining chip while keeping the option of escalation open. Oman said it evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker after it came under attack near Musandam. The risks are no longer limited to ship interceptions or missile attacks. The incident also places Oman before a dual task: protecting a maritime passage adjacent to its coastline and preventing Musandam from becoming a direct flashpoint between Iran and the United States. The key indicator will be whether incidents recur along routes exiting the Gulf, or whether the parties move toward a joint inspection and escort mechanism.

Nomura FX Insights: US Roadshow Notes — Client Views and Nomura's Stance
We distilled several core observations from our client conversations.
The following are several core takeaways from our US client roadshow during the week of October 19, covering global FX and Asian rates markets. Client discussion points covered the following six areas:
1. Overall optimism on US tech stocks over the medium to long term;
2. Some clients have established long USD/JPY positions, believing that the broader backdrop for portfolio flows has not changed;
3. Views on USD/CNH are split, but most clients lean toward CNH appreciating against the USD;
4. Most clients are bearish IDR, neutral TWD, leaning bullish INR, with the strongest bullish sentiment on KRW;
5. Most clients believe US rates are valuation-supported at current levels and that there are safe-haven inflows, though some remain cautious about elevated energy prices;
6. Clients favor receive-fixed trades in Korean rates, but conviction on receive-fixed trades in Hong Kong front-end rates is relatively limited.
Overall, we conclude that the US clients we met have largely not done much positioning for a US equity market correction, which creates downside risk for USD/JPY.
On USD/CNH, after this roadshow, more market participants believe that the downward move in USD/CNH will not only play out over the medium term, but will also materialize faster than implied by FX forward prices.
For the rest of Asian currencies, we agree with the consensus bearish view on IDR, but the buildup of short IDR positions also carries some risk.
We are bearish INR, as the country's balance-of-payments pressure remains; meanwhile, we maintain that Korea and Taiwan will be supported by strong current account surpluses. Given the potential for life insurance fund flows and FX valuation factors, we are relatively more bullish TWD, though we remain cautious due to risks from US equities and the tech sector.
In Asian rates, overall market positioning is not excessively crowded, but trades have tended to be curve flatteners.

US Client Views and Nomura's Thoughts
1. US clients are overall optimistic on US tech stocks over the medium to long term, mainly because they believe capex and earnings at the "Magnificent Seven" will not disappoint before 2027.
Some clients noted these companies have ample cash positions and are not sensitive to rising US yields.

Our stance is relatively cautious; we stress that pressure is gradually building. Bloomberg data on October 14 show that 14.8% of US technology company loans are already distressed (i.e., rates are 10% above SOFR; the total sample size of technology loans is $278.1 billion), and the volume of distressed US technology loans is rising.

At the same time, we note that US high-yield credit default swap spreads have continued to rise over the past month and are already close to the highs seen around the outbreak of the US-Israel conflict earlier this year.

Importantly, even if the medium- to long-term outlook remains optimistic, our high-frequency indicators (ETF and mutual fund flows) show that the scale of foreign investor inflows into US portfolio assets has slowed in recent weeks, which will put pressure on the US equity market and the US dollar.

We also laid out our medium- to long-term bearish US dollar view, on which client pushback has been limited; the rationale includes the following eight points:
a) Large global investors plan asset reallocations to reduce the US asset share;
b) Crowded market positioning combined with technology sector risks;
c) The large US twin deficits create persistent financing needs and pose risks;
d) Concerns over Federal Reserve independence have not been dispelled;
e) The US economy is gradually slowing, and its growth gap with other major economies is narrowing;
f) US midterm election risk, with polling data favoring the Democrats;
g) Real money, pension funds, life insurers and other institutions have potential demand for FX hedging (i.e., selling US dollars);
h) Our judgment of medium- to long-term appreciation in offshore RMB and JPY.

a) Our concerns about the US equity market environment, weakening risk appetite and capital repatriation; there have recently been signs of Japanese investors selling overseas portfolio assets;
b) A change in the FX intervention landscape (i.e., US participation and more active operations);
c) The Bank of Japan's continued gradual monetary policy tightening, with the Japanese 2-year-10-year yield curve flattening, which would limit USD/JPY upside;
d) Improved sentiment among Japanese life insurers toward domestic bonds; narrowing US-Japan policy rate differentials may affect life insurers' hedging ratios, while we need to watch the household sector's medium- to long-term allocation behavior toward JGBs.

We propose a short USD/JPY strategy, with conviction 3/5 and a year-end target of 152.50.

3. Views on USD/CNH are divided, but most clients lean toward offshore RMB appreciation.
No unified consensus has formed to short USD/CNH; some clients note that short USD/CNH carries negative carry, while others believe the market will merely track changes in FX forwards.
Our view differs: the decline in spot USD/CNH has actually significantly exceeded FX forward pricing; over the past year, offshore RMB has appreciated 6.4% against the US dollar; in 8 of the past 12 months, the annualized appreciation ranged from 6% to 17%; on a month-end-to-month-end basis, it outperformed FX forwards in 9 of 12 months.
Our core views include:
a) The scale of FX settlement and FX receipts by exporters is very strong;
b) There is almost no sign that the authorities will suppress RMB appreciation; recent signals show policy efforts to expand the use and internationalization of the RMB, and the People's Bank of China has also stated that the exchange rate's impact on exports is limited;
c) There is international political pressure for a stronger RMB;
d) The RMB itself is highly competitive, with a relative advantage in production efficiency.

We recommend short USD/CNH, conviction 4/5, year-end target 6.50.

a) balance of payments fundamentals are weak, and high oil prices further amplify current account deficit pressure;
b) AI transformation will create hidden concerns for India's software surplus;

iii. On TWD and KRW: most clients focus on the strong current account surpluses of both; market sentiment is more bullish on KRW, and the worst phase of foreign portfolio outflows has passed.

b) if the global tech sector corrects, or if SK Hynix and Samsung shares rise sharply, be alert to the shock from foreign selling of Korean equities; foreign ownership of Korean stocks reached USD 1.6 trillion in September 2026, and a tech selloff would create enormous pressure.

If KOSPI rises sharply, led by SK Hynix and Samsung, KRW would also face multiple risks:
a) single-stock position limits being hit again, forcing funds to sell Korean memory chip stocks (under EU UCITS regulations);
b) overseas investment by Korea's National Pension Service would increase as KOSPI rises;
c) our analysis finds that after local equities strengthen, equity and multi-strategy hedge funds would increase long USD/KRW NDF hedges.

Korea's financial account has other challenges: the Korean retail sector's overseas investment is high (mainly in US assets); Korea's shift in attitude toward Alaska investment, combined with Trump-related policy risks, also warrants attention.

iv. Unless US tech stocks see a larger selloff, we are relatively more bullish TWD; FX valuation shows TWD is significantly undervalued, which could invite US government FX scrutiny, especially compared with KRW, CNH and JPY, which have appreciated in recent months.

At the same time, Taiwan, China will not see the kind of situation in Korea where foreign investors are forced to sell stocks because of single-stock position limits; with hedging ratios low, if the US dollar starts to decline, life insurers in Taiwan, China may restart FX hedging trades that short USD/TWD.

The Gulf's energy-security problem extends beyond the volume of crude oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz.

Liquefied natural gas depends on specialized vessels, terminal infrastructure, reliable shipping routes and predictable delivery schedules.

# The Intermediary's Cut

*Tokenization was supposed to make stocks tradable 24/7. Companies are now asking who ends up controlling the chain.*

Something rarely seen on Wall Street has happened: Nvidia and Walmart, Goldman Sachs and Coca-Cola, Moderna and McDonald's have all taken the same side. Fifty major American companies, including competitors and firms from opposing sectors, have come out against the tokenization of their shares on the exchange planned by OKX and ICE. The list includes tech giants, banks, pharmaceutical makers, and retailers. Companies don't come together this easily; it only happens when there is a shared discomfort.

The promise of tokenization is appealing. Shares become digital units on a blockchain, trading runs seven days a week, twenty-four hours a day, small investors can buy a fraction of a share, and settlement speeds up. In theory, the market becomes more open, more accessible, and cheaper.

The companies' objection is aimed not at the technology but at the structure. Brokerages are the ones carrying out the tokenization. In other words, the new digital guise of the stock brings an old problem with it: the company that issues the share watches someone else step in between itself and the investor. Most of the value generated by trading flows to the brokerages. Under this arrangement, companies don't want to be the party that gets the smallest share from the circulation of their own product.

This concern is not unfounded, but it is not one-sided either. The companies' objection doesn't stem solely from concern for market integrity. They want a say over where, under what conditions, and with whose profit margin their shares trade. They object to their shares becoming a "product" from which they are not the ones profiting. On the other hand, brokerages will argue that they are the party that finances, regulates, and delivers the new technology to investors. No company can reach the investor base without a brokerage.

The real question is this: who will keep the efficiency gains that tokenization brings? The investor, the issuer, or, as always, whoever waits at the gate? Technology sets out with the claim of eliminating intermediaries but often ends up creating new ones. Financial history is full of examples.

The stance of these 50 companies may not decide the fate of tokenization. But the message is clear: what is being contested is not the innovation itself but the distribution of the gains. If the blockchain cannot erase the intermediary, it will end up carrying it to the bargaining table.

Most backtests you see on here are lying to you. Not always on purpose. But a lot are lying.

Here's the biggest trick nobody talks about.

They test with what they know NOW, not what they knew BACK THEN.

Someone backtests "buy the top 10 Nasdaq stocks since 2015" and it looks incredible. But they used TODAY's top 10. $NVDA, $META, all the winners. In 2015 you had no idea those would be the winners. The stocks that blew up and got kicked out of the index? Gone from the test like they never existed.

That's not a strategy. That's hindsight with a chart.

The other ways they fool you

Perfect fills. They assume every trade fills at the exact price on the screen. In real life you miss fills, get re-quoted, and pay the spread. On options that alone can turn a winner into a loser.

No fees. Commissions, exchange fees, settlement fees, data costs. Leave all that out and a losing strategy suddenly looks great.

Cherry picked start dates. Start the test right at the bottom of a crash and anything looks genius.

Curve fitting. Tweak the settings 500 times until the past looks perfect. Then it falls apart the second it trades live.

Only testing bull markets. Everything works when the market only goes up.

A few lucky trades. Take out the 5 best trades and see what's left. A lot of "amazing" strategies are just one or two monster wins carrying everything.

So before you trust any backtest, ask these 6 questions.

1. Did you use the stock list from back then, or today's?
2. Are the fills from real quotes at that minute, or the perfect price?
3. Are every fee and cost included?
4. What happens if you start on a different day? Or the worst day?
5. Does it still work after removing the best 5 trades?
6. Did it survive a real bear market, not just 2023 and 2024?

If they can't answer those, it's not a backtest. It's marketing.

That's the standard I hold my own bots to. Every one of those questions, every start date since 2018, real quotes on every trade, plus stress tests for 2000 and 2008. It's a lot of work, and it's the only way I'd ever put money behind something.

Next time someone shows you a backtest, ask them one question. Did you use what you knew back then, or what you know now?

Most of them won't have an answer.

Around lunchtime Eastern, a well-meaning engineer pushed a "low-risk" change to Azure Front Door. It quietly routed every sign-in on Earth to a SharePoint intranet page titled "Welcome to the New Portal (BETA)," last edited in 2016.

Rollback started right away. Unfortunately, rollback needs MFA approval in Microsoft Authenticator, and Authenticator was waiting on a Conditional Access check from the exact service that was down. The system is now approving itself in a loop and has been promoted to Senior Engineer.

The break-glass admin account was ready. Its password is in an Excel file called passwords_FINAL_v3_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx, saved to OneDrive, on the affected tenant, with AutoSave on.

The on-call engineer reached for PowerShell. The module he needed was retired last Tuesday. Its replacement requires an E5 license, Global Admin, and a blood oath. He's now three tabs deep in Microsoft Learn, and every tab says "This content has moved."

We opened a Severity A case with Premier Support. They asked us to run sfc /scannow, clear our browser cache, and confirm whether the issue happens in an InPrivate window. They also want a screenshot, sent through Outlook.

The fix was approved in principle, but the Change Advisory Board needs a Teams meeting to sign off. The organizer is stuck in the lobby. The only person who can admit him left the company in June and still shows up in the Global Address List with a status of "Be right back."

Mitigation is underway. Affected customers are being moved to Microsoft 365 E5 Premium Plus Copilot Edition, which fixes the outage from a revenue perspective. Copilot has offered to summarize the incident, but it can't reach the incident.

Root cause has been identified as customer misconfiguration, specifically the customer's decision to use Microsoft 365.

The next update is in 30 minutes, if someone can get Outlook to open without asking them to "sign in to continue." The update will be posted on X, because it's the only thing that's up.

WHAT HAPPENED (Fri Nov 13, ET)
CONFIRMED
• 15:10: O'Hare ground stop for "COMMS ISSUES". The nationwide stop followed at 15:54.
• FAA's only stated cause: a "temporary telecommunications outage". DHS Sec. Mullin says there's no sign of an attack so far.
• 20:16: the FAA cancelled the nationwide stop (ATCSCC advisory 005, signed 20:19), 4 hours 22 minutes after it was ordered. The 19:37 plan had listed it to 23:00.
• 20:20–20:23: follow-up advisories (ATCSCC 006–010) cancelled the airport delay programs at LGA, BOS, LAS, SAN and SFO.
• L3Harris runs FTI, the FAA network linking 4,400+ sites (per L3Harris's own site).
REPORTED, NOT CONFIRMED
• Delays and cancellations continue as operations recover. NBC News counted upwards of 5,300 U.S. cancellations Friday (as of 20:16), and FlightAware nearly 800 for Saturday (both via IFR Meter).
• CBS (multiple unnamed sources): an update to the private ATC comms network, operated by L3Harris, made it reboot and crash. L3Harris hadn't commented as of 20:26 ET.

THE TAPE
• Close $272.49 (+0.2% while the S&P ETF fell 0.4%).
• After hours, trading started lower in the 18:15 bar, touched $256.12 (−6.0%) and printed $261.94 at 19:58 (−3.9%), after reports, before any official finding.
• Thin after-hours volume: 9,521 shares in total, about 0.5% of a normal day (30-day avg 1.97M).
• YTD −7.2%. 28% below the $379.23 high (Mar 2), 17% above the $232.34 low (Oct 8).

HOW BIG IS THE FAA BUSINESS?
• Every FAA contract dollar obligated to L3Harris in federal FY26 adds up to $1.52B (USAspending). That's ~6% of the $23.5–23.7B 2026 revenue guide. It's a rough proxy (FY26 FAA obligations, not revenue); FTI revenue isn't broken out in filings.
• It's a fast-growing piece: $681M in FY24, $1.23B in FY25, $1.52B in FY26. The Q3 10-Q credits "higher FAA volume" with +$135M of revenue YTD.
• Separately, L3Harris says 70% of FTI sites are now on fiber.
• The FAA is already replacing the network. Verizon won FENS, FTI's successor, in 2023. In Aug 2026 the FAA made AT&T the prime, targeting end-2028.

FUNDAMENTALS (Q3, filed Oct 29)
• Revenue $6.06B, +7% (+9% organic). GAAP EPS $3.28, +33%.
• Orders $19.3B. Book-to-bill 3.2x. Record backlog $53.2B (it was $40.7B in Q1).
• Missile Solutions book-to-bill was 11.8x, on $6.3B THAAD and $4.7B PAC-3 propulsion awards.
• Q3 FCF $1.26B (+195%). 2026 FCF guide held at $3.0B.
• 2026 EPS guide raised three times: $11.30–11.50 (Jan) → $11.40–11.60 (Q1) → $11.80–12.00 (Q2) → $12.25–12.35 (Q3). Revenue guide raised twice, to $23.5–23.7B.
• Debt $11.0B vs $3.0B of cash and short-term investments. That's ~2.2x net debt/EBITDA.

VALUATION AT $272.49
• 25.4x trailing P/E, 22.2x on the 2026 guide midpoint
• 16.4x EV/EBITDA (EV ~$59.7B)*
• FCF yield 5.9% on guidance (7.2% trailing)
• Street: 15 Buy / 8 Hold / 0 Sell, mean target $336.67
*EV uses the preferred at carrying value ($0.99B) and the Oct 2 balance sheet. With the preferred at redemption value ($1.42B) plus the $1.0B notes issued Nov 5, EV is ~$61.1B, or 16.8x.

OUR TAKE
The FAA is already replacing L3Harris's network. It can't do it fast. The FAA said a fresh FENS competition would take at least 22 months, and the 4,400-site network has to run on L3Harris until cutover. So the near-term FAA revenue is sticky. The real risk is political: hearings, a faster handoff, and a hit to L3Harris's civil air-traffic credibility. None of that changes the $53.2B backlog. The FY27 defense budget still matters far more; the stock fell 6.5% on Nov 4 amid post-midterm budget fears.

WHAT TO WATCH, IF/THEN
• IF the FAA or L3Harris confirms the update caused it: hearing calls, scrutiny of FTI contract terms and service credits (not public), and pressure to pull the AT&T FENS handoff forward.
• IF the cause lands elsewhere or stays vague: FTI keeps running on L3Harris until FENS cutover (end-2028 target), and focus returns to the backlog and the FY27 defense budget.
• THEN watch for a DOT IG review or the FAA pulling FENS work forward. Either would turn a one-night headline into a slow drag on the FAA business.

LATEST: 6,868 people who say they work at Nvidia have signed the petition to bring back Jensen Huang, about 16 percent of the roughly 42,000 staff in its last annual report. The campaign's own method note says their identities and jobs are not verified. No account is needed.

The campaign does not verify job grades either, and signers get no email to confirm who they are.

As of right now on 15th November the letter carried 137,810 names. 

74,088 signed as shareholders, 1,283 as former Nvidia staff and 55,571 as supporters. Those labels are self-reported too.

Uber staff tried this in June 2017. More than 1,100 of them asked the board to return Travis Kalanick in an operational role, and they signed in with their Uber credentials, Axios reported. By late August the board had picked Dara Khosrowshahi as chief executive.

Elon Musk wrote on 13th November, US time, that he was signing it too. The next day he wrote that many of Huang's supply deals "were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract." He added that "at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Nvidia's own numbers show how much sits on paper. Its quarterly report for the 3 months to 26th July puts supply commitments at 279 billion dollars, up from 119 billion dollars one quarter earlier. The filing does not say which of those deals began with a handshake.

The petition asks for something only the board can grant. Nvidia's bylaws let the board fill any officer vacancy. Shareholders can force a special meeting only with 15 percent of the voting power, held for at least 1 year. Huang's 811.5 million shares were about 3.4 percent of the company at his September filing.

Nvidia has published no reply. Its newsroom and its filings show nothing new since the 12th November filing in which the board "accepted the resignation."

It’s highly likely that Nvidia does not name Jensen Huang chief executive again, interim or permanent, or return him to its board, by 31st December 2026. I am wrong if an Nvidia filing or statement does either by that date.

Three "bring back Jensen" letters are now circulating, and it is easy to blend them into one story. They are not the same thing, and one of them is fake.

The real institutional one came Friday evening. Atreides' Gavin Baker posted a joint letter to Nvidia's board, signed with Altimeter's Brad Gerstner - two investors holding about $2.13B of NVDA between them, per CNBC. The ask is narrow: a "slow, measured, and deliberate process" on leadership that "leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang." Kress has their confidence in the interim, and if the board ultimately decides against a return, "that is the Board's prerogative." No accusation, no ultimatum, no demand for reinstatement - just don't rush the replacement.

The second is grassroots. An open letter at https://t.co/ikQfxozgwu passed 150,000 names by Sunday morning, including more than 7,300 self-reported current Nvidia employees, per the site's own counter - signer identities aren't independently verified. Elon Musk says he signed. WIRED separately reports an internal campaign with 1,600+ comments urging the board to find a way to bring Huang back.

The third is fabricated. A letter claiming Nvidia's top executives demanded the board resign was publicly disowned by Nvidia VP Bryan Catanzaro, whose name appears on it: "obviously fake," he wrote, adding that he supports the board and Kress. If that version crossed your feed, discount it entirely.

My read, as judgment rather than prediction: the board can wave off the petition and the fake. The investor letter is harder to ignore - it comes from two large shareholders, it questions the speed of the process rather than the decision, and it gives Kress explicit cover while stopping well short of demanding reinstatement.
